title: Composition of Functions
short: f(g(x)) feeds the output of g into f.
trouble: Students multiply f(x) by g(x), or apply the functions in the wrong order.

blocks.html: In Adding, Subtracting, Multiplying and Dividing Functions you combined two outputs. Composition does something different: the output of one function becomes the input of the next, like two machines on an assembly line.
$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$. Work from the inside out: apply $g$ first, then apply $f$ to the result. To get a formula, replace every $x$ in $f$ with the whole expression $g(x)$.

Read $f(g(3))$ like a set of instructions. The parentheses say $g$ acts on 3 first; its output is the only thing $f$ ever sees. Order matters because the processes are different: putting on socks and then shoes is not the same as shoes and then socks. The little circle $\circ$ is read "after": $f \circ g$ is "$f$ after $g$."

blocks.name: alg2-machines
blocks.cap: Two machines in a row. Change the input and press "Swap the order" to see that $f(g(x))$ and $g(f(x))$ are usually different.

blocks.title: Numbers first
blocks.a: $f(g(2)) = 2$ and $g(f(2)) = 7$: the order changes the answer.

blocks.title: A formula for the composition
blocks.q: With the same functions, find $f(g(x))$ and $g(f(x))$.
steps: Check with $x = 2$: $4(4) - 24 + 10 = 2$ and $2(4) - 1 = 7$, matching the first example.

blocks.html: Multiplying instead of composing. $f(g(x))$ is not $f(x) \cdot g(x)$. In the first example, $f(2) \cdot g(2) = 5 \cdot 1 = 5$, but $f(g(2)) = 2$. Another slip is working in the wrong order. Check yourself by plugging in one number and evaluating step by step from the inside out.
